01 · Introduction

Fire, studied at its source.

Why NASA burns things in space, and what it hopes Earth will gain.

NASA conducts combustion research in space to understand the fundamental physics and chemistry of fire. Its investigations examine gaseous flames, liquid-fuel droplets, solid-fuel ignition, flame propagation, soot formation, combustion efficiency and fire suppression.

Although these experiments are conducted in microgravity, their scientific importance extends to Earth. Understanding combustion more accurately can help engineers develop cleaner-burning systems, improve fuel efficiency, reduce unwanted emissions, improve fire-safety models and design more reliable combustion equipment.

The main scientific advantage of conducting combustion experiments in microgravity is the reduction of buoyancy-driven natural convection. This allows researchers to investigate combustion processes without the strong influence of hot gases rising under Earth’s gravity.

NASA’s research has three broad objectives:

  1. Understand fundamental combustion processes.
  2. Improve fire safety and fire suppression in spacecraft.
  3. Generate experimental measurements and computational models that can support improved combustion technologies on Earth.
Important: NASA’s experiments do not automatically solve terrestrial combustion problems. They provide scientific observations, experimental datasets and model-validation opportunities that engineers can use to develop improved technologies.
02 · Why microgravity

Why test fire in freefall?

Microgravity is a better laboratory for fundamental combustion science: it greatly reduces the buoyant flows that tangle every Earth-based flame test, so researchers can isolate one process at a time and build trustworthy models.

On Earth

Buoyancy stretches the flame upward and drives natural convection. Yellow glow = glowing soot.

In microgravity

Under suitable conditions the flame becomes near-spherical and blue, indicating cleaner, soot-poor burning that is easy to model.

2.1How combustion behaves on Earth

When a flame burns on Earth, it heats the surrounding gases. The heated gases become less dense and rise due to buoyancy. Cooler, oxygen-rich gases move towards the flame.

This movement produces natural convection.

Natural convection influences:

  • Flame shape and size.
  • Oxygen transport towards the flame.
  • Heat transfer.
  • Fuel evaporation.
  • Flame propagation.
  • Soot formation and transport.
  • Flame stability and extinction.

This makes it difficult to isolate certain fundamental combustion processes because chemical reactions, diffusion, heat transfer and convection interact simultaneously.

2.2What changes in microgravity?

In microgravity, buoyancy-driven natural convection is greatly reduced.

Hot gases do not rise in the same way they do on Earth. Combustion is therefore influenced more strongly by molecular diffusion, chemical reactions, heat transfer and any imposed airflow.

This creates an opportunity to study combustion processes under conditions that are difficult to reproduce on Earth.

2.3Advantages of microgravity combustion research

AReduced buoyancy interference

Scientists can investigate the effects of chemical reactions, molecular diffusion and heat transfer without strong buoyancy-driven airflow dominating the experiment.

BMore symmetrical flame structures

Under suitable conditions, flames can become approximately spherical rather than elongated in the upward direction.

This helps researchers investigate flame structure and extinction in different directions.

CBetter investigation of fuel droplets

Liquid droplets can remain suspended for longer without gravitational settling.

Scientists can observe:

  • Droplet evaporation.
  • Fuel-vapour formation.
  • Ignition.
  • Burning rate.
  • Flame extinction.
  • Cool-flame behaviour.

DBetter understanding of flame extinction

Scientists can investigate the conditions under which a flame stops sustaining itself.

These conditions may depend on oxygen concentration, fuel composition, pressure, temperature, heat loss and airflow.

EImproved computational models

Experimental observations can be used to validate mathematical and computational combustion models.

Once validated against appropriate experimental data, these models can be extended to more complicated Earth-gravity combustion conditions.

FUnderstanding unusual combustion phenomena

Microgravity has enabled the investigation of phenomena such as long-duration cool-flame droplet combustion, which is difficult to observe on Earth because the relevant low-temperature reactions are short-lived.

2.4Earth versus microgravity

ParameterEarthMicrogravity
BuoyancySignificantGreatly reduced
Natural convectionOften significantGreatly reduced
Flame shapeOften elongated or irregularCan be approximately spherical
Fuel-droplet movementAffected by gravityGravitational settling greatly reduced
Oxygen transportDiffusion and convectionDiffusion and imposed airflow become especially important
Flame extinctionInfluenced by multiple interacting processesAllows better isolation of some processes
Main scientific advantageRepresents terrestrial combustion conditionsHelps isolate fundamental combustion processes

Microgravity does not eliminate all fluid movement. Forced convection, diffusion and other transport mechanisms still exist.

Why both environments matter: Microgravity experiments help reveal fundamental behaviour, while Earth-based experiments help verify whether the resulting models accurately represent practical terrestrial combustion.
NASA referencehttps://www.nasa.gov/missions/station/iss-research/studying-combustion-and-fire-safety/
03 · The experiments

The real experiments.

The following sections describe real NASA investigations, their scientific objectives, experimental approaches and potential applications to problems on Earth.

3.1Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME)

ACME was a NASA combustion research programme conducted aboard the International Space Station using the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).

Its primary objective was to improve combustion efficiency and reduce pollutant emissions in practical terrestrial combustion systems.

The investigations focused on laminar gaseous non-premixed flames.

A non-premixed flame is one in which fuel and oxidizer are supplied separately and meet in the reaction zone rather than being mixed before combustion.

NASA’s programme descriptions use different groupings: the NASA Science overview describes five core ACME investigations, while NASA’s Glenn documentation also includes the separately identified Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) in its six-investigation programme description.

ABurning Rate Emulator (BRE)

Scientific objective

BRE investigates the flammability of solid and liquid materials by using gaseous fuels to simulate important burning characteristics.

It examines the conditions required for sustained combustion and flame extinction.

It also investigates whether conventional material-flammability testing methods remain suitable for low-gravity and partial-gravity environments.

Problem on Earth

Materials used in buildings, aircraft, vehicles and industrial facilities can ignite and sustain combustion.

Understanding the conditions required for ignition and extinction is important for material safety.

Potential Earth applications
  • Improved material flammability assessment.
  • Better understanding of ignition and extinction limits.
  • Improved fire-risk models.
  • Better evaluation of fire-resistant materials.
  • Improved scientific basis for material-selection standards.

BRE is primarily concerned with spacecraft fire safety, but its fundamental flammability research can also inform terrestrial fire science.

BCoflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame)

Scientific objective

CLD Flame investigates laminar diffusion flames under a wide range of conditions.

It produces experimental benchmark data, including highly diluted and sooty flame conditions, to improve chemical-kinetic and soot-formation models.

Problem on Earth

Combustion in industrial burners and engines can generate soot and other unwanted pollutants.

Poorly understood flame chemistry makes it difficult to predict emissions accurately.

Potential Earth applications
  • Improved soot-formation models.
  • Better industrial burner design.
  • Improved prediction of flame stability.
  • Improved combustion simulations.
  • Better understanding of ignition and turbulent combustion through validated submodels.

CElectric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames)

Scientific objective

E-FIELD investigates how electric fields influence ions generated during combustion and how these ions can be used to control non-premixed flames.

NASA demonstrated the potential of electric fields to reduce emissions from non-premixed flames.

Problem on Earth

Conventional combustion systems may experience unwanted emissions and difficulties maintaining stable combustion across different operating conditions.

Potential Earth applications
  • Electrically assisted combustion control.
  • Investigation of flame stabilization.
  • Improved control of combustion behaviour.
  • Potential reduction of selected emissions.

This research is a potential foundation for advanced combustion-control systems, not proof that all combustion pollutants can be eliminated through electric fields.

DFlame Design

Scientific objective

Flame Design investigates soot formation and control in gaseous diffusion flames.

It studies how flame conditions can be selected to produce robust, soot-free flames and improve oxygen-enriched combustion.

Problem on Earth

Soot is a carbon-rich particulate product of incomplete combustion.

It can:

  • Contribute to air pollution.
  • Cause respiratory health problems.
  • Affect climate.
  • Accumulate in engines and industrial equipment.
  • Reduce equipment performance and increase maintenance requirements.
Potential Earth applications
  • Cleaner industrial burners.
  • Reduced soot production.
  • Improved combustion efficiency.
  • Better understanding of oxygen-enriched combustion.
  • Improved combustion equipment design.

Oxygen-enriched combustion is also relevant to carbon capture research. It can produce exhaust streams with higher CO₂ concentrations than conventional air-fired combustion, potentially simplifying subsequent CO₂ separation.

However, oxygen-enriched combustion alone does not capture or store carbon dioxide.

EStructure and Response of Spherical Flames (s-Flame)

Scientific objective

s-Flame investigates the structure, stability and dynamics of spherical diffusion flames.

It studies both soot-free and sooty flames.

Important research areas include:

  • Flame structure.
  • Flame stability.
  • Flame extinction.
  • Radiative heat loss.
  • Flame instabilities.
  • Pulsating behaviour.
  • Effects of fuel and surrounding gases.
Problem on Earth

Combustion engines and industrial burners require stable flames that operate efficiently and produce fewer unwanted emissions.

Potential Earth applications
  • Improved combustion models.
  • Better prediction of flame extinction.
  • Improved burner stability.
  • Better understanding of lean combustion.
  • Improved engine and industrial combustion design.

FCool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G)

Scientific objective

CFI-G investigates cool flames produced by gaseous fuels in microgravity.

Cool flames are low-temperature oxidation reactions that differ chemically and thermally from ordinary visible hot flames.

CFI-G investigated non-premixed cool flames without enhancements such as heated reactants, pulsed plasmas or ozone addition that had been required in earlier ground-testing approaches.

Problem on Earth

Low-temperature combustion chemistry is important in internal combustion engines and other energy systems, but it can be difficult to study because the relevant reactions are often short-lived.

Potential Earth applications
  • Better low-temperature combustion models.
  • Improved understanding of engine ignition.
  • Research into more efficient combustion strategies.
  • Improved prediction of fuel oxidation.
  • Potential development of cleaner combustion approaches.
Important classification: CFI-G is distinct from the original liquid-droplet Cool Flames Investigation (CFI), which followed the discovery made during FLEX.

Overall importance of ACME

ACME is one of NASA’s most directly relevant combustion programmes for terrestrial energy and environmental problems.

Its research supports improved computational models, cleaner combustion technologies, soot control, flame stability research and reduced pollutant production.

Official NASA referenceshttps://science.nasa.gov/mission/acme/

3.2FLame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX and FLEX-2)

FLEX and FLEX-2 were NASA investigations conducted using the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) inside the Combustion Integrated Rack.

FLEX

Scientific objective

FLEX investigated liquid-fuel droplet combustion and the effectiveness of gaseous fire suppressants in microgravity.

Researchers studied:

  • Fuel-droplet burning.
  • Flame extinction.
  • Oxygen concentration.
  • Suppression by inert gases.
  • Fuel and oxidizer transport.
  • Soot-related processes.
  • Combustion chemical kinetics.

The experiment also supported the development and validation of models describing droplet combustion and extinction.

A major scientific discovery: Cool flames

During FLEX, researchers observed that under certain conditions a fuel droplet continued undergoing low-temperature combustion after its visible hot flame disappeared.

This behaviour became known as cool-flame combustion.

The visible flame extinguished, but chemical reactions continued under certain conditions.

Cool flames are different from conventional hot flames. Their chemical pathways and products can include carbon monoxide and formaldehyde.

This discovery led to the separate Cool Flames Investigation (CFI), which studied the phenomenon in greater detail.

Problem on Earth

Liquid-fuel combustion occurs in:

  • Internal combustion engines.
  • Aircraft engines.
  • Fuel-injection systems.
  • Industrial burners.
  • Other liquid-fuel combustion equipment.
Potential Earth applications
  • Better fuel-droplet combustion models.
  • Improved understanding of ignition and extinction.
  • Improved fuel-injection design.
  • Better low-temperature oxidation models.
  • Improved prediction of combustion emissions.
  • Better understanding of gaseous fire-suppression agents.

FLEX-2

Scientific objective

FLEX-2 extended liquid-droplet combustion research by investigating additional fuel mixtures and combustion conditions.

It examined:

  • Droplet burning rates.
  • Fuel-mixture evaporation.
  • Soot formation conditions.
  • Flame extinction.
  • Combustion behaviour under different environmental conditions.
Problem on Earth

Fuel droplets behave differently depending on their composition, size, temperature and surrounding oxygen conditions.

These factors influence combustion efficiency and emissions.

Potential Earth applications
  • Better liquid-fuel combustion simulations.
  • Improved understanding of multi-component fuel evaporation.
  • Improved fuel-injection research.
  • Better prediction of soot formation.
  • Improved combustion-system design.
Important scientific distinction

FLEX led to the original cool-flame observation. CFI subsequently studied cool flames in detail. FLEX-2 extended droplet-combustion research but should not be described as the original discovery of cool flames.

NASA referenceshttps://www.nasa.gov/missions/station/iss-research/youre-hot-then-youre-cold/
nasa.gov/missions/station/iss-research/studying-combustion-and-fire-safety/ ↗gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/wp/fcf-cir/acme/ ↗

3.3Cool Flames Investigation (CFI)

CFI developed from the unexpected cool-flame observation during FLEX.

Scientific objective

To study the low-temperature oxidation and combustion behaviour of liquid-fuel droplets after the visible hot flame disappears.

Microgravity allows cool-flame reactions to persist for longer under suitable conditions, making them easier to observe and measure.

Problem on Earth

Low-temperature oxidation plays an important role in the combustion chemistry of engines.

Understanding these reactions is important for predicting ignition and engine performance.

Potential Earth applications
  • Improved low-temperature combustion models.
  • Better understanding of engine ignition.
  • Improved fuel chemistry models.
  • Potentially more efficient engine combustion strategies.
  • Better understanding of emissions from low-temperature oxidation.

NASA’s research explains that cool-flame chemistry is relevant to real engines, including processes related to fuel ignition characteristics.

Important: CFI studied liquid-fuel droplets. CFI-G is a separate investigation of gaseous cool flames.
NASA referenceshttps://www.nasa.gov/missions/station/iss-research/youre-hot-then-youre-cold/
psi.nasa.gov/ ↗

3.4Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II)

BASS and BASS-II investigated solid-material combustion in microgravity aboard the International Space Station.

BASS-II was conducted inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) using a small combustion flow duct based on modified SPICE hardware.

Scientific objective

To study:

  • Solid-material ignition.
  • Flame growth.
  • Flame propagation.
  • Burning behaviour.
  • Extinction.
  • Effects of airflow.
  • Effects of oxygen concentration.
  • Effects of fuel thickness and preheating.
  • Nitrogen-based fire suppression.

BASS-II tested different solid samples, including PMMA (polymethyl methacrylate), under controlled airflow and atmospheric conditions.

Problem on Earth

Solid-material fires are important hazards in:

  • Residential buildings.
  • Industrial facilities.
  • Aircraft.
  • Ships.
  • Warehouses.
  • Transportation systems.

The rate at which fire spreads across a solid material depends on material properties, airflow, heat transfer and environmental conditions.

Potential Earth applications
  1. Improved solid-material flammability models.
  2. Better prediction of flame spread.
  3. Improved material fire-safety assessment.
  4. Better understanding of oxygen concentration and fire extinction.
  5. Improved scientific modelling of gaseous suppression methods.
  6. Better evaluation of fire behaviour under different airflow conditions.
Important finding

Microgravity combustion can reveal that solid-material flames behave differently when buoyancy-driven airflow is removed.

The flame can become highly sensitive to small changes in forced airflow.

This is useful for improving computational models of solid-fuel combustion.

NASA referenceshttps://psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/data/investigations/PSI-25
ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20160000593 ↗nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/burning-and-suppression-of-solids-bass.pdf ↗

3.5Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (SAFFIRE I–VI)

Saffire was a series of six large-scale spacecraft fire experiments.

Unlike ACME, FLEX and BASS-II, which used facilities aboard the ISS, Saffire experiments were performed inside uncrewed Cygnus cargo spacecraft after they departed the ISS.

This allowed NASA to investigate larger fire scenarios without exposing astronauts to the experimental fires.

Scientific objective

To investigate fire growth and spread under spacecraft-relevant conditions.

The investigations studied:

  • Flame spread across solid materials.
  • Fire growth.
  • Heat release.
  • Oxygen consumption.
  • Combustion-product generation.
  • Airflow effects.
  • Fire detection and monitoring.
  • Fire behaviour in enclosed environments.

Materials used across the Saffire investigations included:

  • Cotton/fiberglass composite materials.
  • PMMA.
  • Nomex.
  • Other spacecraft-relevant fabrics and materials.
Problem on Earth

Large fires in enclosed environments can occur in:

  • Aircraft cabins.
  • Ships.
  • Trains.
  • Buildings.
  • Industrial facilities.
  • Transportation environments.

Understanding how flames spread and how heat and combustion products accumulate is essential for safety engineering.

Potential Earth applications

AAircraft and transportation safety

Saffire’s experimental observations can contribute to the understanding of fire growth and flame spread in enclosed environments.

BImproved fire-growth models

Heat-release and flame-spread data can support the development and validation of computational fire models.

CMaterial safety

Measurements of the burning behaviour of different materials can help improve fire-risk assessment.

DFire detection

Understanding the production and transport of smoke and combustion gases can support the development and evaluation of fire-detection systems.

EFire suppression

Better understanding of fire development can help engineers evaluate suppression strategies and fire-protection systems.

FPost-fire hazard assessment

Combustion-product measurements can help improve understanding of hazardous gases and environmental conditions after a fire.

Important: Saffire’s primary purpose was spacecraft fire safety. Applications to buildings, aircraft and ships are potential benefits through improved scientific understanding and modelling, not proof that Saffire directly developed commercial fire-safety products.
NASA referenceshttps://www.nasa.gov/centers-and-facilities/glenn/flame-burns-out-on-nasas-long-running-spacecraft-fire-experiment/
ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240002981 ↗psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/data/investigations/PSI-98 ↗

3.6Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction (SoFIE)

SoFIE is a NASA solid-material combustion research facility operating in the Combustion Integrated Rack.

It supports different investigations examining solid-material ignition, flame growth and extinction.

Three important investigation names are:

  • SoFIE-GEL.
  • SoFIE-MIST.
  • SoFIE-RTDFS.

These are separate investigations with different scientific objectives.

ASoFIE-GEL (Growth and Extinction Limit)

Scientific objective

To investigate how the temperature of a solid fuel affects its flammability and the growth and extinction of flames.

It uses thick solid fuel samples, including PMMA spheres.

The experiment investigates:

  • Flow velocity.
  • Oxygen concentration.
  • Pressure.
  • Internal fuel heating.
  • Flame shape.
  • Flame growth.
  • Flame extinction.
Problem on Earth

Understanding how heat penetrates solid materials and influences sustained burning is important for predicting fire growth.

Potential Earth applications
  • Improved solid-material combustion models.
  • Better prediction of flame growth and extinction.
  • Improved material flammability assessment.
  • Better fire-risk simulations.

NASA specifically describes the comparison of numerical models with microgravity results as a way to connect Earth-gravity and microgravity performance.

BSoFIE-MIST (Material Ignition and Suppression Test)

Scientific objective

To investigate thermally assisted burning and the conditions under which solid materials ignite or extinguish.

The experiment uses a PMMA cylindrical fuel sample.

It varies:

  • Airflow speed.
  • Oxygen concentration.
  • Pressure.
  • External radiant heat flux.

It investigates ignition and extinction boundaries under controlled conditions.

Problem on Earth

Solid materials exposed to external heat can ignite and continue burning.

Understanding the interaction between heat flux, oxygen and airflow is important for fire safety.

Potential Earth applications
  • Improved material fire-safety assessment.
  • Better understanding of thermal ignition.
  • Improved fire-growth models.
  • Better scientific evaluation of extinction conditions.
  • Improved combustion simulations.

NASA’s SoFIE-MIST page identifies SpaceX-27 as its delivery mission. SpaceX CRS-27 launched in March 2023. The investigation was subsequently configured on the ISS. Its status should be distinguished from the completion status of the SoFIE programme as a whole.

CSoFIE-RTDFS (Residence Time Driven Flame Spread)

Scientific objective

To investigate flame propagation over solid fuels and the influence of residence time on flame spread.

Residence time describes how long heated gases remain near the fuel surface.

Problem on Earth

The rate of flame spread across solid materials is important in predicting fire growth in buildings and other environments.

Potential Earth applications
  • Improved flame-spread models.
  • Better prediction of solid-material fire behaviour.
  • Improved fire-safety simulations.
  • Better understanding of heat and mass transfer during solid-fuel combustion.
Overall importance of SoFIE

SoFIE produces experimental information that can improve the scientific understanding of solid-material flammability and help validate numerical models.

Its Earth applications include better fire-growth predictions, material assessment and fire-protection engineering.

NASA referenceshttps://science.nasa.gov/biological-physical/investigations/sofie-gel/

04 · The hardware

The hardware behind the flames.

NASA uses specialised experimental hardware to create controlled combustion environments, supply fuel and oxidizer, ignite samples, measure flame characteristics and collect scientific data.

The following are actual facilities and experimental apparatus.

4.1Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)

Purpose

The Combustion Integrated Rack is a dedicated combustion research facility aboard the International Space Station.

It was developed by NASA’s Glenn Research Center and launched in November 2008.

It is located in the U.S. Destiny laboratory module.

Its main feature is a 100-litre combustion chamber that provides a contained environment for combustion experiments.

Capabilities
  • Controlled combustion experiments.
  • Experimental containment.
  • Support for different experiment inserts.
  • Controlled experimental atmospheres.
  • Optical observation.
  • Integration with experimental measurement systems.
Investigations supported
  • ACME.
  • FLEX and FLEX-2 through MDCA.
  • CFI.
  • SoFIE.
Potential Earth applications of research conducted using CIR
  • Improved engine combustion models.
  • Cleaner industrial burners.
  • Better flame-stability predictions.
  • Improved material flammability models.
  • Better understanding of combustion efficiency and emissions.

The CIR itself is a space research facility, not a terrestrial combustion device.

NASA referencehttps://gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/wp/fcf-cir/

4.2Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA)

Purpose

MDCA is a specialised apparatus designed to conduct liquid-fuel droplet combustion experiments.

It operates inside the Combustion Integrated Rack.

It supports different investigations involving isolated fuel droplets.

Experimental capabilities
  • Droplet positioning.
  • Controlled fuel-droplet ignition.
  • Droplet combustion.
  • Flame observation.
  • Investigation of droplet evaporation.
  • Flame-extinction measurements.
  • Study of fuel mixtures and combustion behaviour.
Investigations supported
  • FLEX.
  • FLEX-2.
  • CFI.
  • Other related droplet-combustion investigations.
Potential Earth applications
  • Better fuel-injection models.
  • Improved understanding of droplet evaporation.
  • Improved prediction of liquid-fuel ignition.
  • Better combustion models for engines.
  • Improved understanding of low-temperature oxidation.

4.3ACME Chamber Insert

Purpose

The ACME insert provides the experimental configuration for studying gaseous diffusion flames inside CIR.

It supports controlled delivery of fuel and oxidizer and integration with diagnostic equipment.

Investigations
  • BRE.
  • CLD Flame.
  • E-FIELD Flames.
  • Flame Design.
  • s-Flame.

CFI-G is also included in NASA’s broader ACME research programme descriptions, although its experimental configuration and programme classification should be distinguished from the five core ACME investigations.

Potential Earth applications
  • Soot-reduction research.
  • Cleaner industrial burners.
  • Improved combustion models.
  • Flame stability analysis.
  • Electrically influenced combustion research.

4.4SoFIE Experimental Insert

Purpose

SoFIE is a specialised insert operating inside the Combustion Integrated Rack.

It supports experiments involving solid fuel materials under controlled conditions.

Capabilities
  • Solid-fuel sample testing.
  • Controlled airflow.
  • Controlled oxygen concentration.
  • Controlled pressure.
  • External heating.
  • Electrical ignition.
  • Observation of flame growth and extinction.
Investigations
  • SoFIE-GEL.
  • SoFIE-MIST.
  • SoFIE-RTDFS.
Potential Earth applications
  • Material flammability assessment.
  • Improved fire-growth models.
  • Better understanding of thermal ignition.
  • Improved fire-safety engineering.
  • Better evaluation of extinction conditions.

4.5Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)

Purpose

The Microgravity Science Glovebox provides an enclosed and contained workspace aboard the ISS for scientific investigations.

It has built-in gloves and a sealed working volume, allowing astronauts to handle experimental materials while limiting exposure to the surrounding station.

It was used for BASS and BASS-II.

Capabilities
  • Experimental containment.
  • Handling of solid fuel samples.
  • Support for experimental apparatus.
  • Video and data recording.
  • Controlled experimental workspace.
Potential Earth applications of research conducted inside it
  • Improved fire-spread models.
  • Better material flammability testing.
  • Better fire-suppression research.
  • Improved understanding of solid-fuel combustion.

4.6SPICE/BASS-II experimental hardware

Purpose

BASS-II used modified SPICE hardware installed inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox.

The apparatus consisted of a small combustion flow duct with an igniter, nozzle and exchangeable fuel samples.

Its main components included:

  • Small combustion flow duct.
  • Fuel sample holders.
  • Electrical igniter.
  • Airflow fan.
  • Airflow measurement equipment.
  • Radiometer.
  • Digital camera.
  • High-definition video camera.
  • Nitrogen supply for suppression tests.

The fan produced controlled airflow through the duct, while the anemometer measured the airflow velocity.

The radiometer measured flame output.

The nitrogen supply was used to investigate flame suppression.

Potential Earth applications
  • Better fire-suppression models.
  • Improved solid-fuel flame-spread models.
  • Better understanding of airflow effects.
  • Improved material safety research.

4.7Saffire Flow Unit

Purpose

The Saffire Flow Unit was a specialised experimental enclosure installed inside uncrewed Cygnus cargo spacecraft.

It functioned as a controlled-flow combustion test facility.

Major components and capabilities
  • Fuel sample holder.
  • Controlled airflow.
  • Fan system.
  • Electrical ignition wire.
  • Cameras.
  • Temperature sensors.
  • Pressure measurement.
  • Gas monitoring.
  • Combustion-product monitoring.

The airflow and ignition conditions were controlled remotely.

Potential Earth applications
  • Improved enclosed-environment fire models.
  • Better understanding of heat release.
  • Improved combustion-product monitoring.
  • Improved fire-detection modelling.
  • Better fire-risk assessment.
NASA referencehttps://www.nasa.gov/centers-and-facilities/glenn/flame-burns-out-on-nasas-long-running-spacecraft-fire-experiment/
05 · Measurement

Measuring fire.

Combustion research requires quantitative measurements, not just photographs of flames.

Different NASA experiments use different instruments according to their scientific objectives.

The following are examples of diagnostic equipment documented in NASA combustion research.

5.1High-speed and digital cameras

Used to observe:

  • Flame shape.
  • Flame propagation.
  • Flame extinction.
  • Fuel-droplet behaviour.
  • Flame spread across materials.

Potential Earth application: Validation of computational flame and fire simulations.

5.2Radiometers

Measure radiant energy emitted by flames.

Potential Earth application: Improved heat-transfer and fire-radiation models.

5.3Thermocouples and temperature sensors

Measure temperatures at specific locations in an experiment.

Potential Earth application: Improved thermal models of combustion and fire propagation.

5.4Gas sensors and gas analysers

Depending on the experiment, these measure combustion-related gases, including:

  • Oxygen (O₂).
  • Carbon dioxide (CO₂).
  • Carbon monoxide (CO).

Potential Earth application: Improved understanding of combustion products and environmental hazards.

5.5Anemometers and airflow measurement systems

Measure airflow velocity through an experimental duct.

Potential Earth application: Better understanding of airflow-dependent flame behaviour and fire spread.

5.6Pressure sensors

Measure experimental pressure conditions.

Potential Earth application: Better pressure-dependent combustion models.

Important: Not every instrument listed here is used in every NASA experiment. The actual instrumentation must be verified against each experiment’s technical documentation.
06 · Applications on Earth

Solving Earth’s problems.

Six real-world problems and the experiments, hardware and research that address them.

The following is a consolidated mapping between real Earth problems and relevant NASA investigations.

PROBLEM 1

Air pollution caused by combustion

Earth problem

Combustion can generate soot, particulate matter, carbon monoxide and other pollutants.

Relevant NASA research
  • ACME Flame Design.
  • ACME CLD Flame.

07 · Data to models

From data to predictive models.

NASA experiments generate measurements under specific experimental conditions.

These measurements can be used to develop, calibrate and validate computational combustion models.

A general workflow is:

  1. Obtain actual NASA experimental datasets.
  2. Identify the measured variables and their units.
  3. Understand the experimental conditions.
  4. Clean and organise the data.
  5. Identify relationships between experimental conditions and combustion behaviour.
  6. Develop physical, mathematical or data-driven models.
  7. Compare predictions with actual experimental measurements.
  8. Validate the model using independent experimental cases.
  9. Use the validated model to estimate behaviour under conditions not directly covered by the dataset.

7.1Possible model input variables

Depending on the experiment, potential input variables include:

  • Fuel type.
  • Fuel concentration.
  • Oxygen concentration.
  • Pressure.
  • Initial temperature.
  • Droplet diameter.
  • Airflow velocity.
  • Gravity level.
  • External heating conditions.
  • Fuel composition.

7.2Possible model output variables

Depending on the experimental dataset, possible outputs include:

  • Flame diameter.
  • Flame temperature.
  • Flame spread rate.
  • Burning duration.
  • Droplet lifetime.
  • Droplet burning rate.
  • Ignition conditions.
  • Extinction conditions.
  • Soot concentration.

Not every NASA experiment measures all these variables. The actual dataset schema must be examined before selecting model inputs and outputs.

7.3Important scientific limitation

A model trained using microgravity data must not automatically be considered accurate for Earth-gravity conditions.

Earth gravity introduces buoyancy-driven convection, which changes fluid movement, oxygen transport and heat transfer.

A scientifically reliable model must account for these differences and be validated using appropriate experimental observations under the target gravity conditions.

09 · Rigour

Scientific limits & fact-checking rules.

The following principles must be respected when using NASA combustion research.

  1. Microgravity reduces buoyancy-driven natural convection; it does not eliminate all fluid movement.
  2. Spherical flames form under suitable experimental conditions, not universally.
  3. Microgravity does not automatically make every fire burn more intensely.
  4. The disappearance of a visible hot flame does not necessarily mean that all chemical oxidation has stopped.
  5. Cool flames are low-temperature oxidation phenomena, not ordinary visible flames.
  6. FLEX discovered cool-flame behaviour; CFI subsequently investigated it in detail. CFI-G is a separate gaseous cool-flame investigation.
  7. ACME’s experiment count depends on whether CFI-G is included in the programme grouping. State the classification being used.
  8. NASA’s Saffire investigations primarily address spacecraft fire safety. Terrestrial applications are potential benefits from the resulting science and modelling.
  9. SoFIE-GEL, SoFIE-MIST and SoFIE-RTDFS are distinct investigations.
  10. NASA hardware facilities and individual measurement instruments must not be treated as interchangeable.
  11. Experimental measurements must not be confused with model predictions.
  12. A model validated using microgravity data is not automatically validated for Earth-gravity combustion.
  13. Different investigations use different fuels, geometries, measurement systems and atmospheric conditions. Their datasets should not be combined without checking compatibility.
  14. Potential Earth applications must not be presented as already-commercialised technologies unless there is separate evidence.

11 · Conclusion

Final conclusion.

NASA’s microgravity combustion research is scientifically valuable because it allows researchers to investigate fundamental combustion processes without the dominant influence of buoyancy-driven natural convection.

Experiments such as ACME, FLEX, FLEX-2, CFI, BASS-II, Saffire and SoFIE investigate different aspects of combustion, including gaseous flames, liquid-fuel droplets, cool flames, solid-material ignition, flame propagation, soot formation and fire suppression.

Specialised facilities such as the Combustion Integrated Rack, Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus, Microgravity Science Glovebox, SoFIE insert and Saffire Flow Unit make it possible to conduct these experiments safely and collect scientific measurements.

The resulting research can support:

  • More accurate combustion models.
  • Improved fuel-efficiency research.
  • Cleaner combustion technologies.
  • Reduced soot and unwanted emissions.
  • Better understanding of low-temperature oxidation.
  • Improved material flammability assessment.
  • Better fire-spread and fire-suppression models.
  • Improved fire-safety engineering.

The central scientific principle is:

Studying combustion in microgravity helps scientists isolate fundamental physical and chemical processes. These observations improve scientific models that can subsequently be applied and validated under Earth’s gravitational conditions.

This is the connection between NASA’s space-based combustion experiments and solving combustion-related problems on Earth.
